source_units.heading: Rubric and independence
source_units.text:
## Rubric and independence

Required components: time_profile_and_outcome_units, incremental_employer_return, gift_form_controls_and_mechanism_limits. Each full prompt/key below elicits every component; all are necessary for a pass on every permitted pair. Accept algebraically equivalent expressions and clearly defined opposite cash-flow signs with correct interpretation. A pass requires all requested outputs/reasons, correct units/assumptions and no critical conceptual error. Partial means a missing component or an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip with an otherwise valid method; independent correction is required for a pass. Fail means a critical mechanism/condition is wrong. Unscorable means a response or its help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown help conditions are never independent evidence.

Critical errors: Worker wage confused with funds raised/output; early gain equated with persistence or profit; cash preference assumed to rank effort; 2010/2011 versions mixed; unique mechanism claimed.

Acquisition requires two distinct unused unassisted full checks selected from the six exact metadata routes. ## Immediate and delayed checks

### O010-I1

O010-I1, item_version 1, full_capability_check. **Prompt:** A hypothetical six-hour one-time employment task has four 90-minute blocks. Control output counts are [50, 50, 50, 50]; gift-group counts are [58, 54, 50, 50]. The gift increases hourly wages by 3 currency units for all six hours, and each extra output unit is worth 1 to the employer; other costs are identical. Compute each treatment-control block difference, total extra output and incremental employer net return. Does an early response establish persistence or profitability? Contrast the actual Gneezy–List outcome units/time pattern, the Kube wage-cut asymmetry, and cash/bottle/price-tag/choice/origami controls. Explain why 80% choosing cash can coexist with a larger effort response to a considerate gift and why the results do not uniquely prove one psychological channel.

**Complete solution and essential rubric:** Block differences are $(8,4,0,0)$ output units; extra output is $12$. Incremental revenue is $12(1)=12.00000000$; added wage bill is $6(3)=18.00000000$, so hypothetical incremental net return is $-6.00000000$. The effect fades in this supplied profile; initial, persistent and profitable responses are separate claims. These invented calculations are not a re-estimate of the studies. Gneezy–List compares library books/90 minutes and fundraising money raised per work time (not worker wage); early treatment differences shrink, and the authors’ employer-return conclusion is setting-specific. Kube’s wage-cut group has a larger/more persistent negative response than the positive gift’s advantage; asymmetry is not equal magnitudes with opposite signs. The gift-form study holds employer gift cost near €7 while changing cash/bottle/presentation; the price tag weakens pure price-overestimation, choice distinguishes consumption preference from response to considerate treatment, and origami holds money at €7 while adding care. Roughly 80% cash choice does not require effort to respond most strongly to an unthoughtful cash transfer. The 2011 version has about 25% bottle/choice and 30% origami results; do not substitute the different 2010 version. Attention, perceived kindness, beliefs and reference adaptation remain overlapping explanations; no universal gift elasticity or complete unemployment cause is proved. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

source_units.heading: Explanation steps
source_units.text:
## Explanation steps

Origin: reused complete note introduction before its first subsection, [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/Relative_Pay_and_Charitable_Gift_Exchange.md#Relative pay and charitable gift exchange]], fingerprint `f25609e10a80282755875d6639b5d4cc8b32423bdac3240e176c3a7e277e95ef`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Relative pay and charitable gift exchange

Social preferences can make the treatment of co-workers or donors relevant even when own monetary pay is fixed. The lecture combines a workplace comparison experiment with a fundraising experiment. Their common logic is to vary a socially meaningful feature while keeping a useful monetary benchmark clear. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf#page=25|L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 25–35]]

```mermaid
flowchart TD
 A[Social preferences in field settings] --> B[Compare own wage with co worker wages]
 A --> C[Gift accompanies donation request]
 B --> D[Same own wage under equal or unequal pay]
 D --> E[Output attendance and perceived justification]
 C --> F[Random no small or large gift]
 F --> G[Response probability amount and later giving]
 E --> H[Interpret effect within design and outcome units]
 G --> H
```

This map places the comparison group and outcome denominator before the substantive conclusion. It follows the two supplied applications and prevents treating attendance, donation frequency and donation amounts as interchangeable. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf#page=26|L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 26–34]]

Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/Relative_Pay_and_Charitable_Gift_Exchange.md#Relative wages with own wage held fixed]]; fingerprint `f25609e10a80282755875d6639b5d4cc8b32423bdac3240e176c3a7e277e95ef`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Relative wages with own wage held fixed

Breza, Kaur and Shamdasani's Indian field experiment organizes workers into teams whose members make the same product in proximity, while production remains individual. Teams are assigned either a flat common daily wage or different wages linked to baseline productivity rank. Comparisons across treatments can hold a worker's **own absolute wage** fixed while changing what co-workers receive. Without this comparison, a low-paid worker's lower effort could simply reflect lower own pay rather than relative-pay concerns. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf#page=26|L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 26]]

The lecture reports that workers paid less than peers reduce output by **12%** and are **13% less likely to come to work**, while higher relative pay produces no detected effort increase. These are the lecture's reported percentages, not an instruction to relabel the attendance change as 13 percentage points. Nor does “no detected increase” prove an exactly zero effect for every worker. The Sli.do page asks for a prediction but shows no poll results. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf#page=27|L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 27–28]]

Perceived justification matters: when the pay gap is clearly supported by observed baseline productivity differences, the negative effect is not detected. The simple fact of unequal pay therefore does not fully determine the response; information about why pay differs changes the interpretation. The source concludes that inequality was bad for the firm in the studied comparison. Treat that as an application-specific result, not a general theorem that every wage difference reduces output. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf#page=28|L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 28]]

The lesson links to inequality aversion and fairness perceptions, but the design does not identify one utility function merely from a negative response. A preference for equality, resentment about unjustified treatment and beliefs about management can generate overlapping predictions. The model note also explains why a utility penalty on an entirely effort-independent fixed wage gap cannot mechanically derive every effort effect without an additional channel. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf#page=7|L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 7, 26–28]] [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/Effort_Contracts_and_Social_Motivations.md#Adding a marginal social motive]]

source_units.text:
## Worked example

O011-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. **Prompt:** A hypothetical unequal-pay workplace comparison holds a low-paid worker’s own daily wage fixed across equal-pay and peer-higher-pay teams, with the same individual production task. Baseline output is 100 units; the unequal-pay condition reduces it by 12%. Baseline attendance probability is 0.8; for this hypothetical calculation “13.0% less likely” explicitly means a relative reduction from that baseline. Calculate output, attendance probability and percentage-point change. Explain the identifying comparison, how “the pay gap is visibly explained by prior productivity” would bear on the interpretation, and what the lecture’s actual 12%/13% reports do and do not establish. Does the design identify a unique inequality-aversion utility, or can a constant fixed wage-gap penalty by itself derive effort?

**Complete solution and essential rubric:** Output becomes $100(1-.12)=88.00000000$ units. Under the expressly supplied relative-probability convention, attendance becomes $0.8(1-0.13)=0.69600000$, a change of $-10.40000000$ percentage points. Relative percent and percentage points differ; the lecture’s actual 13% statement cannot be converted to 13 points or a numerical probability without a baseline and precise definition. Keeping own wage fixed while changing peers’ wages separates relative-pay treatment from an own-wage-level explanation, subject to the randomized design and measured task. Clear baseline-productivity justification can change perceived fairness; the lecture reports no detected negative effect under visible justification, not a theorem that any wage gap is harmless. Its 12% output/13% attendance reports are source-reported setting-specific effects and “no detected” high-pay increase is not proof of exact zero. Equality concerns, resentment, fairness beliefs and management intentions can overlap. A literally fixed gap term is constant in effort and has zero derivative; a further effort/payoff or social-meaning channel is needed. No unique utility function or universal employment effect is identified. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

source_units.heading: Explanation steps
source_units.text:
## Explanation steps

Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/Relative_Pay_and_Charitable_Gift_Exchange.md#Falk: a gift before the donation decision]]; fingerprint `f25609e10a80282755875d6639b5d4cc8b32423bdac3240e176c3a7e277e95ef`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Falk: a gift before the donation decision

Falk's 2007 field experiment sends roughly 10,000 letters for an education charity supporting schools in Bangladesh, addressed to potential donors in Switzerland. The randomized treatments contain no gift, one postcard, or four postcards. The postcards are illustrated with a child's drawing; the drawing is part of the gift treatment, not evidence about an individual donor's circumstances. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf#page=29|L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 29–31]]

The theory comparison assumes that the solicitation and recipient's information are otherwise comparable. Pure selfishness without another benefit predicts no donation. Simple altruism about the charity's work alone need not respond to gift size if relevant information and beliefs remain fixed. Reciprocity predicts a stronger response to a larger kind gesture. These predictions depend on the maintained assumptions: gifts might also affect attention, beliefs, warm glow or perceived solicitation costs, so a response gradient is consistent with reciprocity rather than a unique proof of it. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf#page=30|L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 30]]

| Treatment | Letters | Donations | Rounded donation frequency |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| No gift | 3,262 | 397 | 0.12 |
| Small gift | 3,237 | 465 | 0.14 |
| Large gift | 3,347 | 691 | 0.21 |

These source counts sum to **9,846 letters**, explaining why “roughly 10,000” is an approximation. The frequency denominator is all letters in that treatment. A movement from 0.12 to 0.21 is about 9 percentage points, whereas its relative increase using those rounded numbers is about 75%; the two descriptions have different units. Exact ratios calculated from the raw counts need not equal ratios of the rounded displayed frequencies. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf#page=32|L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 32]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/assets/Week_2_Donation_Frequency.png]]

The next histogram shows the distribution of **positive donation amounts**, conditional on giving. It uses a different denominator from the frequency table. A treatment can change how many recipients donate, the amounts donors give, or both. The conditional histogram alone cannot establish the change in average revenue per mailed letter. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf#page=33|L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 33]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/assets/Week_2_Conditional_Donations.png]]


Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/Relative_Pay_and_Charitable_Gift_Exchange.md#Timing and the revenue denominator]]; fingerprint `f25609e10a80282755875d6639b5d4cc8b32423bdac3240e176c3a7e277e95ef`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Timing and the revenue denominator

The source reports these CHF totals and Christmas means:

| Outcome | No gift | Small gift | Large gift |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Christmas 2001 total | 24,673 | 27,106 | 40,877 |
| Christmas mean per letter | 7.56 | 8.37 | 12.21 |
| February 2002 total | 14,023 | 13,206 | 13,165 |
| Combined total | 38,696 | 40,312 | 54,042 |

For example, 24,673/3,262 is about CHF7.56, so the mean is per letter, including recipients who gave nothing, rather than per positive donor. The slide footnote retains donations of at most CHF500 (approximately €350). The February totals are lower in the gift groups than in control, suggesting that timing or substitution must be considered; combined totals still remain higher for the large gift group. Revenue is not net profit: postcard, postage and other treatment costs are not supplied here, so these totals do not establish net returns. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf#page=34|L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 34]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/assets/Week_2_Donation_Followup.png]]

**Bounded verification:** the [publisher abstract for Falk 2007](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-0262.2007.00800.x), *Econometrica* 75(5), 1501–1511, confirms random assignment, approximately 10,000 letters, and the reported 17%/75% relative increases in giving frequency for small/large gifts. Full external paper access was not required for the lecture's reproduced tables and is not claimed here.

Relative pay and charitable gifts are core applications because they test social motivations outside anonymous laboratory games. The important skill is to reconstruct the comparison, prediction, outcome and limitation. The lecture's final summary reports social preferences as relevant in labour and donor contexts; it does not turn each empirical percentage into a universal behavioural constant. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_2/L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf#page=35|L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 35]]

source_units.text:
## Worked example

O012-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. **Prompt:** In a hypothetical randomized charity mailing, no-gift and gift groups each receive 1000 letters. No-gift has 120 positive donors and gift 210. Christmas gross revenue is CHF 6000 versus CHF 10000; later revenue CHF 4000 versus CHF 3000. The gift accompanies the request before the donation decision. Compute response frequencies, the percentage-point and relative-percent change, Christmas average per letter versus per positive donor, combined average per letter, and incremental net return if extra gift cost is CHF 0.5 per gift-group letter and all other costs are identical. Explain what the conditional-positive histogram misses, why timing matters, and which reciprocity versus selfish/altruistic predictions require maintained information/preferences. Distinguish these supplied toy costs from the actual source’s missing net-cost data.

**Complete solution and essential rubric:** Frequencies are $120/1000=0.12000000$ and $210/1000=0.21000000$. Difference is $9.00000000$ percentage points; relative rise is $(0.21/0.12-1)100=75.00000000\%$. Christmas means per letter are $6000/1000=6.00000000$ and $10000/1000=10.00000000$CHF, including zeros; per positive donor they are $6000/120=50.00000000$ and $10000/210=47.61904762$CHF. Combined gross per letter is $10000/1000=10.00000000$ versus $13000/1000=13.00000000$ CHF. Incremental net is $(13000-10000)-1000(0.5)=2500.00000000$ CHF under the hypothetical common-cost assumptions. A positive-donation histogram conditions on giving and cannot alone determine response probability or revenue/letter. Lower later giving can reflect timing/substitution, so Christmas alone is incomplete. Pure selfishness without another benefit predicts no giving; simple altruism alone need not vary with gift size if charity information/beliefs are fixed; reciprocity predicts a gift gradient, but attention/beliefs/warm glow can overlap. The actual Falk table totals 9,846 letters (roughly 10,000), uses counts/rounded frequency denominators and has no supplied treatment costs; its gross totals cannot prove actual net profitability. Gifts accompany solicitation, rather than preceding the request. These calculations are toy outputs, not observed donor results. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

## Misconceptions and correction

An observed omitted term/sign is tentative until the learner explains it; compare the reasoning with the critical errors above. Score the original response before providing help. Route a conceptual failure to the relevant included derivation and prerequisite, then use an unused full form.

O012-C1, item_version 1, narrow_correction. **Prompt:** A histogram shows positive donation amounts only. Can it establish average revenue per mailed letter by itself? **Key/rubric:** No. It conditions on giving; the probability of giving and all-letter denominator are also needed. Treatment costs and later donations are separate ingredients for net returns. Pass requires all keyed reasoning; partial for a missing part; fail for the conflicting mechanism. This repairs a common inference only; it cannot substitute for a full numerical/capability check.

Give at most two hints (first identify the date/unit, second point to the included identity); after ineffective hints show the relevant worked step. After two unsuccessful independent attempts stop repeated quizzing, revisit the explanation/prerequisite and preserve the unresolved status.

source_units.heading: Explanation steps
source_units.text:
## Explanation steps

Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/Social_Preferences_in_Childhood.md#Social preferences in childhood]]; fingerprint `e0a3559c498c69bafe1c4a6d41bffa0c3f527a21fdd89a26affaabf6a221d04b`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Social preferences in childhood

Are preferences fixed traits, or can social experience shape them? This is separate from asking whether preferences are selfish: stable preferences could be other-regarding, and changing preferences could remain selfish. The lecture contrasts a traditional stability assumption, illustrated by Stigler and Becker (1977, p. 76), with a social-environment view attributed to Peter Hedström. Those positions motivate empirical questions rather than establish either answer by assertion. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=1|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 1–4]]

```mermaid
flowchart TD
 A[Separate selfishness from preference stability] --> B[Measure choices in allocation games]
 B --> C[Hold own payoff fixed or make sharing costly]
 C --> D[Compare patterns across three games]
 D --> E[Distinguish equality generosity spite and ambiguity]
 E --> F[Compare age groups and partner group]
 F --> G[Age association with limits on causal interpretation]
```

The map follows the framing, experimental design and results. The core foundation is to derive what each payoff comparison identifies before attaching a preference label to a child. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=2|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 2–16]]

#### Three games distinguish different motives

Fehr, Bernhard and Rockenbach (2008) use anonymous, one-shot allocations of sweets between a child and another child. The lecture describes approximately 250 Swiss children aged 3–8; the consulted Nature paper reports **229 analysed children**, so the lecture's count is approximate rather than an exact sample size. Partners are either classmates from the same school/kindergarten (ingroup) or unknown children from another one (outgroup). The photo shows allocation cards and the group-photo cue identifying partner status; the child does not bargain face to face with the partner. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=6|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 6–7]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/assets/Week_3_Allocation_Setup.png]]

Write a payoff as (own sweets, partner's sweets). The source's tasks are:

| Game | Available allocations | What changes? |
|---|---|---|
| Costless prosocial/sharing | (1,1) or (1,0) | Own sweets stay fixed; helping the partner also removes advantageous inequality. |
| Costless envy | (1,1) or (1,2) | Own sweets stay fixed; equality conflicts with increasing the partner's payoff. |
| Costly sharing | (1,1) or (2,0) | Equality and helping the partner require sacrificing one own sweet. |

A purely selfish child is **indifferent** between the two options in the first two games because own payoff is one in either case; selfishness does not strictly predict one tied option. In costly sharing, selfishness strictly predicts (2,0). A strongly egalitarian child selects equality in all three; a sufficiently altruistic child selects the higher partner payoff, including accepting a cost to share. Spite instead favours reducing the other's payoff. Strength matters when own payoff must be sacrificed. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=6|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 6, 8–13]]

#### Read the whole choice pattern

The source table exhausts the eight combinations of two choices in three games:

| Source classification | Prosocial game | Envy game | Sharing game |
|---|---|---|---|
| Strongly egalitarian | (1,1) | (1,1) | (1,1) |
| Weakly egalitarian | (1,1) | (1,1) | (2,0) |
| Strongly generous | (1,1) | (1,2) | (1,1) |
| Weakly generous | (1,1) | (1,2) | (2,0) |
| Ambiguous type | (1,0) | (1,1) | (1,1) |
| Spiteful | (1,0) | (1,1) | (2,0) |
| Ambiguous type | (1,0) | (1,2) | (1,1) |
| Ambiguous type | (1,0) | (1,2) | (2,0) |

These are the source's behavioural classifications, not infallible personality diagnoses. Because the selfish benchmark permits either costless choice, a child choosing (2,0) in sharing could also produce several of these costless patterns without a strict selfish preference among them. One cannot identify a unique utility function from one tied choice. Consistency, understanding, context and measurement also matter. The four Sli.do pages ask students to predict inequality-averse, altruistic, spiteful and selfish choices; no poll results are supplied, so the reasoning above supplies model predictions rather than invented class responses. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=8|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 8–13]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/assets/Week_3_Preference_Types.png]]

#### The age comparison is conditional on the partner group

The lecture's repeated age figure concerns **ingroup** partners. The proportion making the egalitarian choice in costly sharing rises from about 9% at ages 3–4 to about 22% at 5–6 and 45% at 7–8. The costless prosocial and envy choices reach roughly 78% and 80% at 7–8. These graphical readings show why the lecture describes young children as mostly selfish and older children as more egalitarian, but the costless-game ties mean that label should not be treated as direct proof of a unique motive for every young child. Even among the oldest group, fewer than half choose costly equality. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=14|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 14–15]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/assets/Week_3_Age_Choices.png]]

This is a **cross-sectional age comparison**, not a panel following the same children as they grow. It supports an age-related pattern, not a causal estimate of ageing or a particular upbringing. Its ingroup caption also prevents generalizing the displayed percentages to unknown outgroup children. The lecture's statement that later development includes efficiency concerns and altruism is attributed only to unspecified “different studies”; no unprovided later-age evidence or effect size is certified here. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=14|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 14–16]]

**Bounded primary check:** Fehr, Bernhard and Rockenbach, “Egalitarianism in young children,” *Nature* 454 (2008), 1079–1083, [publisher proof](https://www.nature.com/news/2008/080827/pdf/nature07155_proof2.pdf), physical pp. 1–2 and methods on p. 6, verifies the three tasks, sample count, anonymous one-shot design and ingroup interpretation. The proof distinguishes costless choices from costly sharing; numerical source figures remain tied to their displayed partner condition. This is supporting verification, not ingestion of the paper's entire additional outgroup analysis.

The next question is whether family background is merely associated with preferences or whether changing a child's social environment can alter measured prosociality. Distinguishing those two claims is the foundation of the mentoring application. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=16|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 16–18]] [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/Social_Environment_and_Mentoring.md]]

source_units.text:
## Worked example

O013-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. **Prompt:** In the source’s own/partner-sweets order, the prosocial game offers (1,1)/(1,0), envy game (1,1)/(1,2), sharing game (1,1)/(2,0). A hypothetical child chooses [(1, 1), (1, 1), (1, 1)] in that order. Derive what varies/what is held fixed in each game, the selfish indifference/strict-choice predictions, and the strong-equality/generosity/spite interpretations. Give the table’s classification for this observed pattern and explain whether it uniquely identifies utility or a permanent personality trait. Interpret the age graph’s about 9/22/45% costly-equality pattern, ingroup restriction, anonymous one-shot design and 229 analysed versus approximately 250 sample wording without turning age association into causal development.

**Complete solution and essential rubric:** Own payoff stays 1 in the first two games; changing the partner’s payoff also changes equality. In the third, selecting (1,1) costs one own sweet relative to (2,0). Pure self-interest is indifferent over the first two pairs and strictly prefers (2,0) in sharing. Strong egalitarianism selects equality throughout; sufficiently strong generosity raises the partner’s payoff even when costly, and spite favours reducing it (strength matters with own costs). The source-table label for [(1, 1), (1, 1), (1, 1)] is “strongly egalitarian.” The costly-equality choice sacrifices an own sweet and therefore does not follow from the pure-selfish strict sharing prediction. A behavioural table classification is not a unique utility/personality diagnosis; comprehension, context and ties matter. The actual tasks are anonymous one-shot incentivized sweets allocations, with ingroup/outgroup cues rather than face-to-face bargaining. The displayed age figure is ingroup-only, roughly 9%, 22%, 45% costly equality across 3–4, 5–6, 7–8; even the oldest mean is below one half. It compares different children by age, not a panel or randomized upbringing, so neither causal ageing nor a universal outgroup pattern follows. The primary paper reports 229 analysed children; the slide’s approximately 250 is approximate. Unspecified later-age studies and empty poll prompts are not certified results. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

source_units.text:
## Rubric and independence

Required components: three_payoff_comparisons_and_selfish_ties, whole_pattern_classification_and_identification, age_partner_sample_and_causal_limits. Each full prompt/key below elicits every component; all are necessary for a pass on every permitted pair. Accept algebraically equivalent expressions and clearly defined opposite cash-flow signs with correct interpretation. A pass requires all requested outputs/reasons, correct units/assumptions and no critical conceptual error. Partial means a missing component or an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip with an otherwise valid method; independent correction is required for a pass. Fail means a critical mechanism/condition is wrong. Unscorable means a response or its help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown help conditions are never independent evidence.

Critical errors: Selfishness strictly selects one costless tied option; one choice uniquely diagnoses personality; age cross-section called longitudinal/causal; ingroup percentages generalized to outgroup; approximate 250 treated as exact.

Acquisition requires two distinct unused unassisted full checks selected from the six exact metadata routes. ## Misconceptions and correction

An observed omitted term/sign is tentative until the learner explains it; compare the reasoning with the critical errors above. Score the original response before providing help. Route a conceptual failure to the relevant included derivation and prerequisite, then use an unused full form.

O013-C1, item_version 1, narrow_correction. **Prompt:** A child picks equality when own payoff stays 1. Does that alone rule out pure self-interest? **Key/rubric:** No. Pure self-interest is indifferent between the equal and unequal costless options. Pass requires all keyed reasoning; partial for a missing part; fail for the conflicting mechanism. This repairs a common inference only; it cannot substitute for a full numerical/capability check.

## Immediate and delayed checks

### O013-I1

O013-I1, item_version 1, full_capability_check. **Prompt:** In the source’s own/partner-sweets order, the prosocial game offers (1,1)/(1,0), envy game (1,1)/(1,2), sharing game (1,1)/(2,0). A hypothetical child chooses [(1, 1), (1, 2), (1, 1)] in that order. Derive what varies/what is held fixed in each game, the selfish indifference/strict-choice predictions, and the strong-equality/generosity/spite interpretations. source_units.heading: Prerequisites and checks
source_units.text:
## Prerequisites and checks

- [O001 outcome and repair route](../lessons/O001.md#outcome-and-conditions): the experimental intervention/control contrast is distinct from a background association.
- [O013 outcome and repair route](../lessons/O013.md#outcome-and-conditions): allocation patterns and tied choices limit one-to-one preference interpretations. The trust-survey and observer-rating distinctions are taught in the included O014 foundation below, before its diagnostic or assessed forms.

### Included O014 measurement and index foundation

Read this bounded foundation before O014-P1 and the worked example. The checked passage “What “prosociality” measures” below distinguishes an incentivized dictator allocation (a choice), a trust survey (stated beliefs about others’ trustworthiness, intentions or reliability), and a mother rating (an observer questionnaire). These are different measurements; neither a choice nor a stated belief uniquely identifies every social preference. O013 supplies allocation-pattern and tie reasoning, not the trust-survey distinction. If the measurement part of P1 fails, repair it here and in that complete included checked passage; repair random-assignment reasoning through O001.

For the hypothetical arithmetic in this lesson, let $z_A,z_T,z_M$ denote the three component scores after each component has been standardized. Define the **mean-component-z index** as $J=(z_A+z_T+z_M)/3$. Its treatment-minus-control contrast is the arithmetic mean of the three supplied component contrasts. Report that contrast and any supplied benchmark gap in the same **mean-component-z index units**. Standardizing the components does not give their average a standard deviation of one: the average’s variance depends on their variances and covariances. A subsequently standardized composite would instead require the composite’s own reference mean and standard deviation, for example $Z_J=(J-\mu_J)/\sigma_J$ with $\sigma_J>0$. Those reference quantities are not supplied, so no composite-SD conversion is requested or inferred. This is a transparent explanation of the toy index definition, not a re-estimate of the study’s empirical effect.

O014-P1, item_version 1, prerequisite_diagnostic. **Prompt:** What does random assignment compare, and why is a dictator allocation not identical to a survey statement about trusting others?

**Complete key and rubric:** Random assignment compares assigned intervention/control under its design, not automatically every background difference (O001). An incentivized allocation measures a choice while a trust statement records a belief; neither uniquely identifies every social preference (included O014 measurement foundation and the complete “What “prosociality” measures” passage below). Require both; repair O001 for assignment reasoning and the included O014 foundation for measurement, before retrying. Pass requires every requested reason and result; partial for an omitted reason or unresolved isolated arithmetic slip; fail for the conflicting mechanism. This diagnostic never counts as acquisition. Current or explicitly compatible committed independent prerequisite evidence may permit skipping its check; familiarity alone cannot. Use the cited complete prerequisite lesson or the named included foundation, then the worked example, after a partial/failing entry check.

source_units.heading: Explanation steps
source_units.text:
## Explanation steps

Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/Social_Environment_and_Mentoring.md#Social environment and mentoring]]; fingerprint `ae2f09f4c9e0e3456e9ab1d7fa9303e2c945ea69c2509f71dfb0ef966c7c4d9b`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Social environment and mentoring

Can a policy change measured social preferences, rather than simply predict which children differ? The lecture combines background correlations with a randomized mentoring intervention. Keeping those comparisons separate is essential: a treatment can identify the effect of an offered program without proving that all background differences are caused by one family characteristic. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=17|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 17–23]]

```mermaid
flowchart TD
 A[Measure child prosociality in several ways] --> B[Observe SES and mother child associations]
 A --> C[Randomly offer mentoring among eligible low SES children]
 B --> D[Association does not isolate parental causation]
 C --> E[Compare assigned low SES treatment and control]
 E --> F[Estimate effect of program offer]
 F --> G[Compare measured gap with high SES benchmark]
 G --> H[Qualify equivalence mechanism and generalization]
```

The map follows the supplied experiment and distinguishes the descriptive and causal routes. Random assignment applies within the eligible low-SES sample; it does not randomly assign socioeconomic status (SES). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=18|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 18–23]]

#### The intervention and comparison groups

The lecture attributes the study to Kosse et al. (2020). Primary-school children in Germany are offered a one-year mentoring program: mentors, typically university students, meet children weekly for activities such as museums, the zoo, playgrounds, reading, cooking or conversation. The program enriches social interactions and introduces a potential prosocial role model. The three displayed groups are low-SES treatment, low-SES control and high-SES control. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=18|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 18]]

**Bounded design verification:** the [authors' May 2018 HCEO working paper](https://humcap.uchicago.edu/RePEc/hka/wpaper/Kosse_Deckers_Pinger_etal_2018_formation-prosociality_revised.pdf), §2.1 and §3.4, physical pp. 7–9 and 25–26, verifies stratified random offers among eligible interested low-SES families in Bonn/Cologne. Not everyone assigned obtained or completed mentoring, so the primary comparison is an **intention-to-treat effect of the offer**, rather than the effect of successful participation for every child. High-SES families form a benchmark, not a randomly assigned SES treatment. The later publication is *Journal of Political Economy* 128(2), 434–467 (2020); the lecture's final 2018 citation refers to a working-paper version of this research.

This distinction matters for policy interpretation. The offered treatment includes implementation constraints such as mentor availability. Comparing participants selected by successful matching could lose the protection of random assignment; comparing all assigned groups keeps the offer-based causal question clear. Source slides alone do not supply the compliance details, so this paragraph labels their bounded verification explicitly. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=18|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 18, 21]]

#### What “prosociality” measures

The lecture uses three facets: **altruism**, measured through incentivized dictator allocations; **trust**, measured with three survey statements about whether other people can be trusted, have good intentions and can be relied on even when not known well; and **other-regarding behaviour**, rated by the mother in an everyday-behaviour questionnaire. An incentivized allocation, a stated belief and an observer report measure related but distinct things. Trust is not inferred solely from the amount donated in a dictator game. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=19|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 19]]

The main figure uses an equally weighted index of standardized altruism, trust and other-regarding measures. A standardized score measures position relative to its reference distribution in standard-deviation units, rather than a number of sweets or euros. Combining measures can reduce dependence on one noisy elicitation, but it does not make the three measures identical. Error bars in the supplied charts are standard errors of group means; significance markers refer to stated comparisons, not a test of every bar against zero. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=20|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 20–22]]

#### Background correlations

The first graph shows a higher average child-prosociality index in the high-SES control group than in the low-SES control group. Its second panel shows higher child scores when maternal prosociality is above its median than below. The supplied caption marks the SES contrast at the 5% level and the maternal-prosociality contrast at 1%; the stated sample sizes are 424 and 410, with the latter difference attributed to incomplete mother questionnaires. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=20|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 20]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/assets/Week_3_Background_Associations.png]]

These are associations. They do not distinguish inherited influences, shared environment, parenting, selection, reporting differences or other correlated inputs. The slide's “transmission” language should therefore not be read as a causal estimate of maternal preferences or SES. The differences are group averages, not a characterization of every child or household in either group. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=20|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 20, 23]]

#### The offer changes measured outcomes

The intervention chart shows higher prosociality among low-SES children assigned treatment than among low-SES controls, marked at the 1% level. It reports no statistically significant difference between treated low-SES children and the high-SES control benchmark. The lecture calls this closing the measured gap: the low-SES treatment mean moves toward that benchmark. A nonsignificant difference does **not** prove exact equality or a formal equivalence margin. The causal comparison is treatment versus control within the randomized eligible sample; the cross-SES comparison describes the resulting gap. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=21|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 21]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/assets/Week_3_Mentoring_Treatment.png]]

The component graphs show higher treatment means for altruism, trust and mother-rated other-regarding behaviour. The first two contrasts have 5% significance markers; the third has no significance star. Thus the slide's broad “robust across multiple measures” statement means directionally supportive component patterns, not three separately confirmed significant effects. A positive but imprecisely estimated component is not evidence of an exactly zero effect, either. Caption sample sizes differ because of missing answers or failed control questions. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=22|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 22]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/assets/Week_3_Mentoring_Measures.png]]

#### Mechanism and policy limits

The lecture proposes that children imitate and internalize behaviour from parents and social role models. The working paper's abstract and §3.3 report a mediation analysis supporting prosocial attachment figures and intensive social interaction. This is a proposed interpretation with additional assumptions; randomizing the whole mentoring offer does not separately randomize every mechanism. The intervention's causal effect is stronger evidence than the background correlations, but it does not prove that role-model imitation is the only channel. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=18|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 18, 23]]

The evidence shows that measured prosociality can respond to social environment during childhood. It does not establish that genes are irrelevant, that all socioeconomic differences are environmental, or that this intervention works equally for all ages, countries or outcomes. Its economic relevance is that prosocial behaviour can influence cooperation and other interactions, making the formation of preferences and possible remedial policies worth studying. The closing “why should economists care?” prompt invites that connection; it supplies no observed learner answer. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=23|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 23]]

Experimental comparisons, outcome measurement and causal interpretation are core foundations. The particular program, demographic groups and chart values are applications through which to learn that reasoning, with no unsupported claim about exact exam coverage. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_3/L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf#page=18|L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 18–23]]

source_units.heading: Worked example
source_units.text:
## Worked example

O014-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. **Prompt:** For an explicitly hypothetical eligible low-SES sample, a mentoring offer is randomly assigned against control. Standardized treatment-minus-control component means are altruism 0.3, trust 0.6, mother-rated other-regarding behaviour 0; define the mean-component-z index as their equal-weight arithmetic mean, with no further composite standardization. The high-SES benchmark mean-component-z index is 0.35 mean-component-z index units above low-SES control. Compute the offer’s index difference and remaining benchmark gap. Only 60% of those offered complete participation; why is the assignment contrast still an ITT effect and why can participant-only comparisons lose protection? Suppose the reported index contrast is significant, altruism/trust are starred, mother-rating is unstarred, and treated-low versus high-SES is nonsignificant: interpret without inventing zero/equivalence or a genetic/mechanism conclusion. State what each facet measures, the background-correlation comparison and the actual program’s scope.

**Complete solution and essential rubric:** Mean-component-z index difference is $(0.3+0.6+0)/3=0.30000000$ mean-component-z index units, without an assumed composite standard deviation of one; remaining high-benchmark gap is $0.35-0.30000000=0.05000000$ in the same mean-component-z index units. Further composite standardization would require the composite’s own reference mean and standard deviation, which are not supplied. These are invented arithmetic inputs, not a re-estimate. Randomization is of the offer within eligible interested low-SES families; comparing all assigned preserves the intention-to-treat question even with 60% completion. Completed participation is selected after assignment; its comparison can reintroduce selection, and dividing by participation is not automatically a valid causal participation estimate without further assumptions. High versus low SES and mother-child correlations are descriptive, not randomized SES or parental transmission. Altruism uses incentivized dictator allocations, trust uses stated beliefs about others’ trustworthiness/intentions/reliability, and the mother rating is an observer questionnaire; standardization/equal weighting does not make them identical. Unstarred does not prove zero; nonsignificance versus high SES does not prove exact equality or formal equivalence. The source component stars support the first two contrasts, not three separately significant effects. The actual one-year German mentoring offer involves weekly interactions/role models in an eligible voluntary sample, with implementation/compliance limits. Randomizing the whole offer does not isolate one mediator, rule out genes or establish universal effects across countries/ages/outcomes; it shows measured prosociality can respond to social environment. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

## Practice with fading assistance

O014-S1, item_version 1, supported_completion. **Prompt:** For an explicitly hypothetical eligible low-SES sample, a mentoring offer is randomly assigned against control. source_units.text:
## Rubric and independence

Required components: measurement_index_and_benchmark_arithmetic, random_offer_itt_vs_participation_and_ses, significance_mechanism_and_generalization_limits. Each full prompt/key below elicits every component; all are necessary for a pass on every permitted pair. Accept algebraically equivalent expressions and clearly defined opposite cash-flow signs with correct interpretation. A pass requires all requested outputs/reasons, correct units/assumptions and no critical conceptual error. Partial means a missing component or an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip with an otherwise valid method; independent correction is required for a pass. Fail means a critical mechanism/condition is wrong. Unscorable means a response or its help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown help conditions are never independent evidence.

## Misconceptions and correction

An observed omitted term/sign is tentative until the learner explains it; compare the reasoning with the critical errors above. Score the original response before providing help. Route a conceptual failure to the relevant included derivation and prerequisite, then use an unused full form.

source_units.heading: Behavioral economics and experimental economics
source_units.text:
# Behavioral economics and experimental economics

How should economics explain choices when people care about fairness, have difficulty following through on plans, overlook information, or hold inaccurate beliefs? Behavioral economics answers this question by changing particular assumptions about decision-making while retaining economic modeling and testable predictions. Week 1 introduces that approach and distinguishes it from experimental economics, the method used to gather much of the course's evidence. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=2|Introduction, PDF slides 2–3, 5–6]]

Return to [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Behavioral_Economics_main.md#Week 1|the course's Week 1 section]].

## What changes in a behavioral model

Behavioral economics uses variants of traditional economic assumptions, often motivated by psychology, to explain and predict behavior and inform policy. The lecture also calls it *psychology and economics* or *psychological economics*. The word “behavioral” does not mean that other economists ignore behavior. It identifies the use of psychological insights, particularly cognitive psychology and social psychology, to improve assumptions about how people make choices. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=2|Introduction, PDF slide 2]]

The lecture presents this as amendments to traditional economics. Economic models still need precise, falsifiable predictions: predictions that evidence could show to be wrong. Broadening the assumptions is useful when it explains observed choices more accurately, rather than merely making a story sound plausible. Perfect rationality is one classical assumption that the lecture says need not be retained in every model. It does not claim that every traditional model fails or that mathematical modeling should be abandoned. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=3|Introduction, PDF slide 3]]

The lecture identifies five directions for amendments. They concern different parts of a decision, so they should not be collapsed into a single claim that people are “irrational.” The explanations below unpack the lecture's categories; the introduction does not yet provide their formal models. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=3|Introduction, PDF slide 3]]

| Direction in the lecture | What part of a choice it brings into view |
|---|---|
| Broader motivations: fairness, social preferences, group identity, social norms | A person's motivation can include the treatment of others or expectations associated with a group, alongside their own material outcome. |
| Imperfect self-control | Carrying out a plan can itself be difficult; an intended choice and a later action need not coincide. |
| Imperfect attention | Information can be available without receiving the decision-maker's attention. |
| Inaccurate beliefs | The decision-maker's view of the situation can differ from the relevant facts. |
| Preferences may not be fixed | The motivations used to explain choices need not be treated as unchanging. |

These categories organize later lectures rather than establish particular empirical results in Week 1. For example, a fairness explanation and an inaccurate-beliefs explanation change different elements of the model. Distinguishing them matters because a prediction or policy recommendation depends on the mechanism being proposed. This is a synthesis of the lecture's separate categories and its requirement of falsifiable predictions. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=3|Introduction, PDF slide 3]]

## A field of questions and a method of evidence

**Behavioral economics** concerns the assumptions and explanations used to understand choices. **Experimental economics** is an empirical method that often tests those explanations. Calling an investigation experimental identifies how evidence is generated; it does not by itself identify the behavioral assumptions of the model being tested. The lecture deliberately separates the two terms. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=5|Introduction, PDF slide 5]]

Historically, economists often observed naturally occurring economic processes. Their advantage is that the processes can be studied in their undisturbed form. Their difficulty is causal interpretation: if two observed variables move together, that association alone does not tell us whether changing one would change the other. The lecture contrasts this with an experiment, where the researcher can control information, incentives, and context to estimate causal effects and investigate counterfactual scenarios. A **counterfactual** asks what would happen under an alternative situation, including one that did not occur in the naturally observed process. This explanation follows the contrast on slide 5; the slide does not specify a full identification strategy or an estimator. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=5|Introduction, PDF slide 5]]

The distinction matters when reading research. First ask which behavior the model seeks to explain and which assumption it changes. Then ask how the evidence allows the proposed explanation to be tested. An observed association may be informative without establishing the causal effect required by a policy argument. Experimental control offers a way to get closer to causal effects; the introduction does not say that every experiment automatically resolves every problem of interpretation. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=5|Introduction, PDF slides 5–6]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/assets/Introduction_slide_06_correlation.png]]

*The source's correlation-and-causation cartoon illustrates the caution.* A person reports changing their belief after a statistics class. A second person treats that sequence as evidence that the class caused the change; the reply leaves that inference uncertain. The sequence is compatible with the causal explanation, but the cartoon gives no comparison showing what the person would have believed without the class. This is an interpretation of the displayed illustration, not a research result. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=6|Introduction, PDF slide 6]]

## Theory, evidence, and applications in this course

The course's stated lecture sequence combines theory or intuition, evidence mostly from controlled experiments, and applications to issues such as rewarding employees, tackling poverty, and discrimination. Microeconomics I is the prerequisite because a learner needs the conventional framework with which to compare behavioral amendments. The [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/Course_Organization_and_Exam.md|organization and exam note]] records the study requirements and separates later-topic exam examples from the material taught here. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=9|Introduction, PDF slides 9–10]]

**Agent-created illustration of the course's sequence:** an investigation of how to reward employees can begin with a proposed motivation, derive a prediction about behavior under different incentives, and then ask whether evidence supports it. The lecture supplies the employee-reward application and the theory–evidence–application sequence. This illustration supplies no claim about an actual experiment, wage effect, or preferred policy. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=9|Introduction, PDF slide 9]]

## Week 1 synthesis

Behavioral economics broadens assumptions about motivations, self-control, attention, beliefs, and preferences while requiring testable economic predictions. Experimental economics supplies a frequently used method for testing those predictions and estimating causal effects through control of the research environment. The two concepts answer different questions: what explains a choice, and how can evidence test that explanation? Detailed social-preference models and the later applications are outside this introductory material. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=3|Introduction, PDF slides 3, 5–6, 8–9]]

## From the introduction to social preferences

The introductory categories above are developed further in the additional Social Preferences presentation. [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/Ultimatum_and_Dictator_Games.md|Ultimatum and dictator games]] provides the benchmark and laboratory patterns; [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/Models_of_Social_Preferences.md|Models of social preferences]] gives the utility functions and curve interpretation; [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/Trust_and_Cooperation_Games.md|Trust and cooperation games]] connects those motivations to surplus and cooperation. These pages extend the current Week 1 collection while preserving the scope of the original introductory material described here. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=12|Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 12–14, 23, 37]]

The distinction matters when reading research. First ask which behavior the model seeks to explain and which assumption it changes. Then ask how the evidence allows the proposed explanation to be tested. An observed association may be informative without establishing the causal effect required by a policy argument. Experimental control offers a way to get closer to causal effects; the introduction does not say that every experiment automatically resolves every problem of interpretation. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=5|Introduction, PDF slides 5–6]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/assets/Introduction_slide_06_correlation.png]]

*The source's correlation-and-causation cartoon illustrates the caution.* A person reports changing their belief after a statistics class. A second person treats that sequence as evidence that the class caused the change; the reply leaves that inference uncertain. The sequence is compatible with the causal explanation, but the cartoon gives no comparison showing what the person would have believed without the class. This is an interpretation of the displayed illustration, not a research result. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=6|Introduction, PDF slide 6]]

## Theory, evidence, and applications in this course

The course's stated lecture sequence combines theory or intuition, evidence mostly from controlled experiments, and applications to issues such as rewarding employees, tackling poverty, and discrimination. Microeconomics I is the prerequisite because a learner needs the conventional framework with which to compare behavioral amendments. The [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/Course_Organization_and_Exam.md|organization and exam note]] records the study requirements and separates later-topic exam examples from the material taught here. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=9|Introduction, PDF slides 9–10]]

**Agent-created illustration of the course's sequence:** an investigation of how to reward employees can begin with a proposed motivation, derive a prediction about behavior under different incentives, and then ask whether evidence supports it. The lecture supplies the employee-reward application and the theory–evidence–application sequence. This illustration supplies no claim about an actual experiment, wage effect, or preferred policy. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=9|Introduction, PDF slide 9]]

source_units.heading: Week 1 synthesis
source_units.text:
## Week 1 synthesis

Behavioral economics broadens assumptions about motivations, self-control, attention, beliefs, and preferences while requiring testable economic predictions. Experimental economics supplies a frequently used method for testing those predictions and estimating causal effects through control of the research environment. The two concepts answer different questions: what explains a choice, and how can evidence test that explanation? Detailed social-preference models and the later applications are outside this introductory material. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L1 BE_Introduction IES 2026 v2.pdf#page=3|Introduction, PDF slides 3, 5–6, 8–9]]

source_units.heading: Two assumptions that the lecture brings into question
source_units.key: 01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/Models_of_Social_Preferences.md#Two assumptions that the lecture brings into question
source_units.text:
## Two assumptions that the lecture brings into question

The lecture contrasts broader motivations with two traditional assumptions. **Selfish preferences** make utility a function only of one's own payoff; without reputation-building, the benchmark does not add concern for another person's treatment or fairness. **Exogenous preferences** treat motivations as largely fixed traits, unresponsive to personal experiences or environmental factors. These are distinct claims: including another person's payoff changes the content of utility, while allowing preferences to respond to experience concerns where preferences come from. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=13|Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 13]]

The presentation develops the first issue through payoff weights and behavior-dependent reciprocity. It does not estimate how preferences evolve over a lifetime or provide a formal preference-formation model. Its motivation is that social preferences can support cooperation and economic surplus, linked in the lecture to social capital. “Can” matters: some broader motivations, such as spite or negative reciprocity, also permit costly harm. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=13|Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 13, 18–19, 22, 37]]

source_units.heading: Ultimatum and dictator games
source_units.text:
# Ultimatum and dictator games

Do people maximize only their own monetary payoff when choosing how to divide money? The ultimatum game and dictator game isolate different parts of this question. In the ultimatum game, the recipient can reject an allocation; in the dictator game, the recipient has no such power. Comparing them helps distinguish the effect of threatened rejection from willingness to give when rejection is impossible. Both are introduced as anonymous, incentivized laboratory decisions, rather than hypothetical evidence about what every person always does. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=2|Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 2–3, 8–11]]

Return to [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Behavioral_Economics_main.md#Week 1|Behavioral Economics — Week 1]]. The experimental-method distinction is developed in [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/Behavioral_and_Experimental_Economics.md|Behavioral and experimental economics]].

## The ultimatum game's sequence and payoffs

The **ultimatum game (UG)** has two players, a proposer and a receiver. The proposer is given a fixed monetary pie and chooses a split. The receiver then accepts or rejects. Acceptance implements the split; rejection leaves both players with nothing. The source specifies a one-time, anonymous interaction: the receiver does not know, and will not learn, the proposer's identity. Participants are paid according to their choices. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=2|Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 2–3]]

**Notation and payoff accounting unpacked from the setup:** let $M>0$ be the pie and $r\in[0,M]$ the amount offered to the receiver. Acceptance gives monetary payoffs

$$
(x_P,x_R)=(M-r,r),
$$

where $P$ labels the proposer and $R$ the receiver. Rejection gives $(0,0)$. Thus an offer is not a completed transfer: the receiver has a veto. Rejecting a positive offer is costly to the receiver as well as the proposer. This opportunity to impose a cost is the central difference from the dictator game. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=3|Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 3]]

The lecture's example uses $M=\text{CZK }500$ and asks whether the receiver would accept offers of CZK 0, 1, 20, 100, 150, 200 or 250. The corresponding proposer shares are 500, 499, 480, 400, 350, 300 and 250. These are choice prompts, not observed decisions. The slides also ask for the receiver's minimum acceptable offer and the selfish-model prediction; the exported poll slides contain no responses or results. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=3|Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 3–7]]

## Deriving the self-regarding benchmark

**Self-regarding preferences** make a player's utility depend only on that player's own monetary payoff. The benchmark also assumes the proposer expects the receiver to be self-regarding. To solve the sequential game, reason from the receiver's decision backward to the proposer's offer. This is the lecture's comparison with a **subgame-perfect equilibrium**: a strategy prediction that remains optimal at the later decision stage, including after an offer has actually been made. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=5|Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 5, 8]]

For any $r>0$, a purely monetary receiver gets $r$ from accepting and zero from rejecting, so acceptance is strictly better. A proposer who anticipates this wants to retain as much as possible and offer next to nothing. The lecture summarizes the prediction as an almost-zero offer that is accepted. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=8|Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 8]]

**Qualification derived from the payoff comparison:** at exactly $r=0$, acceptance and rejection both give the receiver zero. Pure self-interest alone therefore leaves the receiver indifferent at zero. An exact minimum offer depends on the allowed monetary unit and how that tie is resolved. If whole CZK offers are allowed and zero would be rejected, the smallest strictly profitable accepted offer is CZK 1. If zero is accepted, offering zero can be optimal. The source supplies neither a tie rule nor a complete offer grid, so its “next to nothing” prediction should not be turned into an unconditional unique zero-offer result. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=3|Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 3, 7–8]]

## Typical ultimatum results and what they challenge

The lecture reports that the modal offer—the most common offer—is 40–50% of the pie, with very few offers below 20%. Offers below 20% are rejected very often, more than 50% of the time in the stated summary. It says these patterns have been replicated many times and differ substantially from the self-regarding subgame-perfect prediction. These percentages are the lecture's reported typical laboratory patterns, not a class-poll result or a universal rate for every design and population. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=8|Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 8]]

The rejection of a positive amount is particularly informative: the receiver gives up money to prevent the unfavorable split from being implemented. [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/Models_of_Social_Preferences.md|Social-preference models]] explain how concern about relative payoffs or treatment can make such an action attractive even though it reduces monetary income. The observed action challenges the purely monetary benchmark under the stated setup; it does not by itself identify one unique preference model. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=8|Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 8, 20–22]]

A positive proposer offer is also not sufficient evidence of altruism. **Reasoning from the game's veto:** even a self-interested proposer can offer more when expecting a low offer to be rejected. The offer may reflect concern for the receiver, anticipation of costly rejection, or both. This is why the dictator game's removal of the veto is useful. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=3|Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 3, 8–9]]

## The dictator game removes the receiver's veto

The **dictator game (DG)** also has a proposer and receiver and a fixed pie, but the proposer’s chosen split is simply implemented. The receiver is completely passive. There is no acceptance or rejection stage. With the same notation, the implemented monetary payoffs are $(M-r,r)$. A strictly self-regarding proposer therefore chooses $r=0$, because every positive transfer directly reduces their own payoff and cannot avoid a receiver veto. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=9|Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 9]]

The lecture describes a typical laboratory implementation with a \$10 pie supplied by the experimenter, participants randomly assigned to proposer and receiver roles, and anonymity about individual decisions or pairings. The endowment is received rather than earned. These procedural features matter when interpreting what the comparison does and does not hold constant. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=9|Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 9]]

The stated typical results are that more than 60% of participants transfer a positive amount, with a mean transfer of roughly 20% of the endowment. The fraction of people giving something and the average fraction of the pie given are different quantities: a 20% mean does not mean that 20% of participants give or that every giver transfers exactly 20%. For the stated \$10 endowment, 20% is about \$2 as an arithmetic illustration, not a separately observed result. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=11|Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 11]]

The lecture stresses sensitivity to procedural details: when the endowment is earned rather than received from the experimenter, giving diminishes. It does not provide a numerical size for that reduction. Positive giving therefore supplies evidence against complete monetary selfishness for many participants in the described setting, while its level depends on the experimental procedure. It does not establish that all participants are unselfish or that these laboratory averages directly predict giving in every other setting. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=9|Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 9, 11]]

## Reading the two games together

| Feature | Ultimatum game | Dictator game |
|---|---|---|
| Who chooses the split? | Proposer | Proposer |
| Can the receiver reject? | Yes; rejection gives both zero | No; the split is implemented |
| Self-regarding proposer benchmark | Offer next to nothing that will be accepted | Give zero |
| What positive giving can reflect | Social concern and/or anticipated rejection | Giving without a receiver veto |
| What the source reports | Substantial offers and frequent rejection of very low offers | Many positive transfers; giving sensitive to the endowment procedure |

The comparison isolates the receiver's strategic power, while the lecture's reported results show that many choices need a broader account of motivation. The next step is to define what “broader” means: [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/Models_of_Social_Preferences.md|Models of social preferences]] separates altruism, spite, inequality aversion and reciprocity. [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/Trust_and_Cooperation_Games.md|Trust and cooperation games]] then examines settings where behavior can change the total monetary surplus, instead of only dividing a fixed pie. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Behavioral_Economics/Week_1/L2 BE_SocPrefs IES 2026.pdf#page=3|Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 3, 8–13, 23–24]]
